explain.tweet: “What caused God?” assumes the argument says everything has a cause. It doesn’t. It says things with unrealized potential, parts, or contingency need a cause — and concludes to the one thing with none of those. Asking what caused it is asking what caused the uncausable.
explain.elevator: Most objections to the First Cause argument attack a version nobody ever defended — “everything has a cause, so the universe has a cause.” The real arguments say something narrower: things that change, have parts, or could have been otherwise depend on something else, right now. Follow that dependence up and you must reach something with no such features. That’s why “What caused God?” misfires, why the universe can’t be the stopping point, and why the question isn’t about the Big Bang at all.
explain.twoMinute:
Here’s something surprising. The most famous objection to arguments for God — “If everything has a cause, what caused God?” — is aimed at an argument that, as far as anyone can tell, no major philosopher ever made. Aristotle, Aquinas, Leibniz, modern defenders like Swinburne and Craig: none of them starts from “everything has a cause.” Even a critic, Robin Le Poidevin, admits no one has defended that version. It got into the textbooks, Feser argues following W. Norris Clarke, because Hume ran together two senses of “cause” — “explanation” and “outside producer” — and generations of critics copied him.

What the arguments actually say is more careful. Things need a cause *because of a specific feature*: they have potentials that something must actualize; they’re made of parts something must hold together; what they are doesn’t guarantee that they are; they could have been otherwise. Trace that dependence and you reach something that lacks the feature — pure actuality, no parts, existence itself, necessary. So asking “What caused God?” is asking what actualized the potentials of the thing with no potentials. It’s not a clever question; it’s a confused one.

The same test handles the next objection: “Why not stop at the universe, or the Big Bang, or the laws of physics?” Because every one of those has the very feature that made us look for a cause — they change, have parts, and could have been different. And if the universe somehow were necessary and self-explaining, you’d have made it divine: that’s pantheism, not atheism.

Most other objections fail in similar ways. “Why assume a beginning?” — the arguments don’t; they’re about what keeps things existing now. “Quantum events are uncaused” — at most they’re not deterministic. “God of the gaps” — these aren’t probabilistic guesses competing with physics; they start from what any physics presupposes. “A universe from nothing” — the physicists’ “nothing” is always space, energy, or laws, which are something.

None of this proves the arguments are right. It shows the popular objections never touch them. The real debate is about the premises — and that’s a much more interesting conversation.
explain.eli12:
Imagine a line of kids passing a ball. You ask, “Where did the ball come from?” Someone says, “From the kid before.” And that kid? “From the kid before him.” Even if the line were endless, you’d still wonder where the ball came from, because none of the kids *made* it — they only passed it along.

Some people argue for God like this: everything we see only *passes along* its existence and its power. It changes, it’s made of parts, it could have been different. So there must be something that doesn’t just pass existence along, but *has* it on its own.

A common reply is, “Then who made God?” But that’s like asking, “Who gave the ball to the person who *made* the ball?” The whole point was that there has to be someone who didn’t get it from anyone.

Other people say, “Maybe the universe is the one who made the ball!” But the universe is just more kids in the line — it changes and is made of parts, so it’s passing things along too.

And when someone says, “Scientists showed the universe came from nothing,” check what they mean. Usually it’s “empty space with energy and rules.” That’s not nothing — that’s a whole lot of something!
whiteboard: Write at top: “Everything has a cause → what caused God?” Cross it out and write: “No major defender ever argued this.” Say: first check whether the objection is aimed at the real argument.
Draw four columns labelled Aristotelian / Neo-Platonic / Thomistic / Rationalist. Under each, write the feature that makes things need a cause: potential, parts, essence ≠ existence, contingent.
Under each column draw an arrow up to the first cause and write what it lacks: pure act, simple, essence = existence, necessary. Say: God’s uncausedness is the conclusion, not an exception.
Write “What caused God?” next to the arrows and rewrite it as “What actualized the potentials of what has no potentials?” Let the audience see it doesn’t make sense.

Draw a box labelled “Universe / Big Bang / multiverse / laws” and tick all four features in it. Say: every rival candidate has the very features that need a cause — and if it didn’t, it would be divine (pantheism).

Draw two chains: a horizontal one (dominoes over time, labelled per accidens, “may be beginningless”) and a vertical one (hand–stick–stone, labelled per se, “needs a first member now”). Say: the multiverse and “laws all the way down” replies attack the horizontal chain; the argument is about the vertical one — and stacked laws are vertical.
Write “CHANCE / QUANTUM / CONCEIVABLE” and under each a short rebuttal: needs crossing causes; not deterministic ≠ uncaused; triangle without “three-sided”.
Draw a row of mirrors with no face. Ask: does explaining each mirror by the next explain the image? Label: the composition fallacy is Grayling’s, not the theist’s.
Write two headings: “God of the gaps (probable, replaceable)” vs “Metaphysical demonstration (necessary, presupposed by all physics)”. Put the proofs in the second.
Finish with “NOTHING = no space, no energy, no laws” and cross out Krauss’s three candidates one by one. Close: the real debate is about the premises.
explain.keyAnalogy: **The borrowed-money chain.** If everyone in a line pays with money borrowed from the next person, lengthening the line — even infinitely — never explains where the money came from; somewhere someone must *have* money without borrowing it. Use it three ways: (1) it shows the hierarchical, here-and-now structure of the arguments (the question is not how long the line is but whether anyone has underived money); (2) it shows why “What caused God?” misfires (“Who lent money to the one who didn’t borrow?”); and (3) it shows why the universe, the multiverse, or an endless stack of laws can’t be the answer — they are just more borrowers. Caveat to add: the “money” is existence and causal power, and the lender is not one more person in the line but the source outside it.

persuade.coreInsight:
The idea that makes this chapter click is that **the arguments never say “everything has a cause.” They say “everything of a certain kind needs a cause”** — whatever has potentials that must be actualized, parts that must be combined, an essence that doesn’t guarantee its existence, or contingency — and then show that the chain of such things must terminate in something *not* of that kind. Once someone sees this, “What caused God?” dissolves, “Why not stop at the universe?” gets an obvious answer (the universe is of that kind), and the per se chain makes the beginning of time irrelevant.

It usually fails to click for two reasons. First, the caricature is so entrenched — in textbooks, popular books, and even professional philosophy — that people hear the real argument *through* it: whatever you say, they file it under “everything has a cause.” Second, people picture causation as a line of dominoes stretching back in time, so a “first cause” sounds like the first domino. You must replace that picture with a vertical, here-and-now picture (hand–stick–stone, the borrowed-money chain) before any of the replies make sense.

In conversation, the most persuasive posture is calm and generous: don’t mock the objection (Feser’s rhetoric is sharp; yours need not be). Acknowledge that it’s the objection everyone learned, explain in one sentence why it misses, and immediately redirect to the real premise — which gives the person something serious to push on.

audiences.who: New Atheist reader (has read Dawkins, Hitchens, or Harris)
audiences.startingPoint: Believes “What caused God?” and “god of the gaps” are knock-down answers; assumes theistic arguments are pre-scientific guesses.
audiences.approach: Start by agreeing that the version they learned *is* bad — then show it isn’t the argument. Mention that even critics like Le Poidevin admit no one defends it, and use the Darwinism “monkey gave birth to a human” analogy so they feel the unfairness from their own side. Then present one real premise (e.g., things that change are having potentials actualized by something else, now) and let them test it. Keep every reply short: the one-liners in this module are ideal.
audiences.openingQuestion: “Before we go further, can you find me one major defender of the argument — Aquinas, Leibniz, anyone — who actually starts from ‘everything has a cause’?”
audiences.avoid: Don’t sneer at their authors; they’ll defend them reflexively. Don’t load them with jargon before the core picture (dependence here and now) is in place.

audiences.startingPoint: Thinks explanation means scientific explanation; treats quantum indeterminism, the multiverse, and Krauss’s “nothing” as serious answers; values precision.
audiences.approach: Honor their precision. Distinguish indeterministic from uncaused; point out that quantum events presuppose quantum laws and systems. Ask what they think laws of nature are — descriptions, abstract entities, or summaries of how things behave — and walk through why none is an ultimate explanation. Frame the proofs as asking what *any* physical theory presupposes (change, composition, contingency), not as rivals to physics.
audiences.openingQuestion: “When you say the laws of physics explain the universe, what do you think a law *is* — a description of a regularity, or something that makes the regularity happen?”
audiences.avoid: Don’t dispute the physics. Don’t imply that science is suspect; the point is that metaphysical questions are a different kind, not that physics is wrong.

audiences.who: Philosophy student (has read Hume and Russell)
audiences.startingPoint: Knows the conceivability argument, the fallacy of composition, and Kant’s ontological-argument objection; thinks these are settled.
audiences.approach: Engage the arguments on their own terms: the triangle/trilateral counterexample and Anscombe’s underdescription point against Hume; the sticks, mirrors, and geometry books against the composition charge; the three kinds of necessity against Kant and Grayling. Introduce W. Norris Clarke’s genealogy (Descartes and Spinoza’s “cause” as sufficient reason) — students often enjoy discovering that the textbook story is historically wrong.
audiences.openingQuestion: “Hume says we can conceive an effect without a cause. Can you conceive a triangle without thinking of it as three-sided? What follows?”
audiences.avoid: Don’t overclaim that the objections are stupid; say they are mistaken and show where. Don’t skip the per se / per accidens distinction — without it the student will keep hearing “first domino.”

audiences.who: Believer who uses the bad version
audiences.startingPoint: Argues “everything has a cause, so God exists” and is thrown when someone asks what caused God.
audiences.approach: Gently correct: the argument they are using is the straw man. Teach them the principled criterion (what makes something need a cause) and the vertical chain. Give them the one-liners for the top five objections so they can answer calmly instead of defensively. Encourage humility: the arguments establish God’s existence and nature, not a particular religion — that’s a further conversation.
audiences.openingQuestion: “When someone asks you what caused God, why do you think God doesn’t need a cause — what’s different about him?”
audiences.avoid: Don’t shame them for the caricature — it’s in half the textbooks. Don’t let them overstate what the arguments prove (the Trinity objection is right that they don’t).

audiences.who: Agnostic who likes “maybe it’s just a brute fact”
audiences.startingPoint: Comfortable with mystery; thinks “we don’t know” is the humble answer and that demanding explanation everywhere is presumptuous.
audiences.approach: Respect the humility but show the special pleading: they would never accept “maybe it has no explanation” for a mysterious illness or a crashed plane. Add Gerson’s point: an explanation is on the table, so “maybe there’s none” is not a reason to reject it. Then show that the argument is not a gap-filler but concerns what any explanation presupposes.
audiences.openingQuestion: “If your doctor said your symptoms might just have no cause at all, would you accept that — or get a second opinion?”
audiences.avoid: Don’t push for a quick conversion; aim for them to see that brute-fact agnosticism is a choice needing justification, not a neutral default.

audiences.startingPoint: Happy to say the universe itself is divine or self-sufficient; resists a personal, transcendent God.
audiences.approach: Point out that Feser agrees the “universe is necessary” move would produce pantheism rather than atheism — so they already accept that *something* necessary and uncaused exists. Then ask whether the universe can really be that something, given it changes, has parts, and could have been different. Mention that the attributes (unity, intellect, will) are argued for in chapter 6.
audiences.openingQuestion: “If the universe is the uncaused, necessary foundation of everything — isn’t that just what people have always meant by ‘God’? So the question is whether the universe fits the job description.”
audiences.avoid: Don’t treat pantheism as the enemy; treat it as a halfway house that already concedes the key point.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: The First Cause argument is simple to refute. If everything has a cause, what caused God?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: That would refute an argument that said everything has a cause. But none of the classic versions says that — not Aristotle, not Aquinas, not Leibniz. Even Le Poidevin, an atheist philosopher of religion, admits no one has defended that version.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Then what does it say?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: That some things need a cause because of a specific feature — say, they have potentials that something else must actualize, like water that can boil only if something heats it. Follow that dependence and you have to reach something with no unactualized potential at all. That thing isn’t exempted from a rule; it’s the thing the rule doesn’t apply to by its nature.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Sounds like you’ve defined God into being the exception.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: It’s the conclusion, not a definition. Try asking the question in the argument’s terms: “What actualized the potentials of the thing with no potentials?” It doesn’t make sense. You can argue that nothing could be pure actuality — that’s a real objection — but “what caused it?” isn’t.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Fine, but why not stop at the universe? If something can be uncaused, why not the universe or the Big Bang?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Because the universe has exactly the features that made us look for a cause: it changes, it’s made of parts, and its laws could have been different. The Big Bang itself was a potential being actualized. And if the universe really were necessary and self-explanatory, you’d have made it divine — that’s pantheism, not atheism.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: What about the laws of physics? They explain everything else.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: What do you think a law is? If it’s just a description of how things regularly behave, it describes rather than explains. If it’s an abstract entity, we need to explain why the world follows it. If it’s a summary of how things behave given their natures, it depends on those things. On none of those views is it the bottom level.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Maybe there’s no bottom. Krauss says there could be layers of laws forever.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Then each layer holds only because a deeper one does — that’s a chain of borrowed power, like money borrowed from the next person forever. More borrowers never produce a lender. That’s the kind of series the argument is about.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Anyway, quantum mechanics shows things happen without causes.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: It shows some events don’t have deterministic causes. That isn’t the same as no cause — a uranium atom decays at a characteristic rate because of what it is and the laws it falls under. And those laws are part of what needs explaining.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Hume pointed out we can imagine something popping into existence with no cause. So it’s possible.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: I can think of a triangle without thinking “three-sided,” but no triangle lacks three sides. And what in your imagined scene makes it uncaused rather than caused by something invisible, or teleported? To make that distinction you end up appealing to kinds of causes.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Okay, but this is just a god of the gaps. Science keeps closing gaps; this one will close too.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: A gap argument says, “We can’t explain this yet, so probably God.” This argument says any physical explanation will itself involve change, parts, and contingency — so it can’t be the last word. Future physics won’t remove that; it will give us more of it.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Hawking said that because there is a law like gravity, the universe can create itself from nothing.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: But a law like gravity isn’t nothing. Krauss’s “nothing” turns out to be space with energy, then quantum laws, then layers of laws — he admits each isn’t really nothing. Nothing is just the absence of anything.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Even so, you’d only get some first cause. Nothing about omniscience or goodness, let alone Jesus.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: The attributes are argued for at length — Aquinas spends hundreds of pages on them, and Feser’s chapter 6 does too. The Trinity is a separate question, you’re right. But if the argument works, atheism is off the table and the question becomes which theism is true.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: So what would a real objection look like, in your view?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Something like: “Pure actuality is incoherent” or “the premise that change requires an actualizer is false.” Those engage the argument. I’d genuinely enjoy that conversation — want to start with the premise about change?

socratic: When someone asks “What caused God?”, what premise are they assuming the argument uses? Can you find that premise in Aquinas or Leibniz?
Why does water need something to heat it before it boils? Is it because “everything has a cause,” or because of something specific about the water?
If a thing had no unrealized potential at all, what would there be for a cause to do to it?
Does the universe change? Does it have parts? Could its laws have been different? What follows if it has those features?
If the universe were uncaused, necessary, and self-explanatory, how would it differ from what people have meant by “God”?
Can you think of a triangle without thinking of it as three-sided? Does that make a two-sided triangle possible?
If a physicist found that a lab phenomenon seemed to have no cause, would she conclude it has none — or keep looking? Why treat the universe differently?
If every copy of a book was copied from an earlier copy, forever, have we explained why the book says what it says?
If each layer of physical law holds only because a deeper layer does, does adding more layers ever supply a layer that holds on its own?
Is empty space full of energy and governed by laws the same as nothing? What would “nothing” have to lack?
Does a proof failing to establish the Trinity show that it fails to establish a First Cause? What would the analogous inference say about physics?

What is the difference between an argument that says “God is the most probable explanation” and one that says “no other explanation is possible in principle”? Which kind is vulnerable to future science?

traps.trap: Defending the straw man — answering “What caused God?” by saying “God is the exception” without explaining why.
traps.fix: Reject the premise first (“the argument never says everything has a cause”), then give the principled criterion: things need causes because of potentiality, composition, essence–existence distinction, or contingency, which God lacks.

traps.trap: Letting the conversation become about the Big Bang or whether time had a beginning.
traps.fix: Concede the point for argument’s sake: “Suppose the universe is infinitely old.” Then move to the vertical, here-and-now picture — what keeps it existing now?

traps.trap: Matching the objector’s contempt. Feser’s tone is sharply polemical; copying it in person usually ends the conversation.
traps.fix: Give the one-line reply calmly, acknowledge the objection is widespread and understandable, and invite engagement with the real premise.

traps.trap: Disputing the science (quantum mechanics, cosmology) instead of the philosophy.
traps.fix: Grant the physics fully; show the philosophical conclusion drawn from it doesn’t follow (indeterministic ≠ uncaused; space with energy ≠ nothing).

traps.trap: Overclaiming: suggesting the First Cause argument proves Christianity or a particular religion.
traps.fix: State plainly that the arguments aim at the existence and nature of God only; what follows about revelation is a separate inquiry.

traps.trap: Treating “necessary being” as “exists by definition” when explaining it, which invites Kant’s objection.
traps.fix: Explain necessity in terms of nature: no potential, no parts, essence identical to existence — so nothing in it could fail to exist.

traps.trap: Answering every objection at length, turning a conversation into a lecture.
traps.fix: Use the module’s one-liners, then ask a Socratic question that hands the conversation back.

traps.trap: Dismissing sophisticated objections (e.g., the coherence of divine simplicity) along with the popular ones.
traps.fix: Distinguish misfires from genuine objections. Welcome the latter as the conversation Feser says a serious critic should be having.

connections.note: The introduction announces chapter 7’s aim — new objections plus deeper treatment of old ones — and predicts the most common objections will prove remarkably feeble. It also frames the book’s two-stage structure (a first cause, then its divine attributes), which the “no reason to think it’s God” objection ignores, and says the real debate is among theists of different kinds — exactly Feser’s reply to “it doesn’t prove the Trinity.”

The per se / per accidens distinction and the sticks and mirrors from the Aristotelian proof are the key tools here — against “why must the regress end?”, the multiverse, Krauss’s layers of laws, and the fallacy-of-composition charge. The act/potency criterion answers “What caused God?” and “why not the universe?”.

The Neo-Platonic criterion (composition requires a cause; the absolutely simple doesn’t) is one of the four principled answers to “What caused God?”, to the universe-as-terminus objection, and to Grayling’s charge that metaphysical necessity is merely relative.
Feser’s footnote sets the Augustinian proof aside: since it isn’t a causal argument, “What caused God?” isn’t even superficially relevant to it.

The Thomistic criterion (essence distinct from existence needs a cause; subsistent existence doesn’t) answers the universe objection and grounds non-definitional necessity against Kant — with the footnote that God’s essence *is*, not merely “includes”, existence.

PSR and the contingency criterion answer “maybe there’s no explanation”; chapter 5’s discussion of the fallacy of composition (red Lego bricks; Leibniz’s geometry books) is reused against Grayling; Descartes’ and Spinoza’s “self-caused” God is read as a PSR claim.

Chapter 6’s account of divine necessity (not definitional) is what defeats the claim that the cosmological argument presupposes the ontological one; its arguments for unity, simplicity, and immutability answer “why think the first cause is God?”.

The derivations of omnipotence, omniscience, and goodness in the second half of chapter 6 are the book’s answer to Dawkins’, Grayling’s, and Krauss’s claim that there is no reason to ascribe such attributes to a first cause. Chapter 6 also argues against pantheism — relevant to this module’s point that making the universe the necessary being would yield pantheism rather than atheism.

The second half of chapter 7 continues the same diagnostic approach against scientism, the appeal to laws of nature, “who designed the designer?”, the Zeus/Thor comparison, the “God of the philosophers,” evil, divine hiddenness, the rationalization charge, and “no one can prove God exists.” The critique of laws of nature begun here is developed there.

The capstone’s conversation practice should draw on this module’s one-liners and the misfire diagnosis: restate what the argument claims, name the test the objection fails, and redirect to the real premise.
